chapters.title: Chapter 3: TDS on Investment Income and Other Payments

lessons.title: TDS on Rent, Commission and Freelance Professional Fees

body.text: If you earn rent, commission or freelance fees, TDS is a slice of your own income that the payer sends to the government first. You get it back only as a credit months later, so know the rate and threshold for every payment and track every certificate.

children.text: Nikhil is a freelance architect in Bengaluru. Sudha, 63, a retired bank officer in Indore, rents out a shop she inherited. They have never met, but they share a problem: money they earned is regularly withheld before it reaches them, at rates that have nothing to do with their actual tax. This lesson covers TDS on the four payments self-employed people and landlords meet most often: rent, commission, professional fees and contract work.
The Rules at a Glance
All of these now sit in the tables of Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The rates and thresholds below apply to resident payees with a valid PAN in tax year 2026-27.

body.text: The payer decides which row applies, and the same kind of work can be read differently. Software development, for example, is sometimes treated as professional fees (10%), sometimes as technical services (2%) and sometimes as contract work (1% or 2%). If a client picks a rate you think is wrong, raise it early. Over-deduction is refunded eventually, but under-deduction becomes the client's problem and can sour the relationship.

children.text: Landlords: Rent From a Business

Sudha rents her shop to a pharmacy chain, a private limited company, for ₹75,000 a month. Because that exceeds ₹50,000 a month and the tenant is a business, it deducts 10% every month: she receives ₹67,500 and ₹7,500 goes to the government against her PAN.

body.title: Try It: Sudha's TDS for the Year
body.prompt: Sudha's tenant pays ₹75,000 a month for all 12 months of tax year 2026-27 and deducts TDS at 10%. How much TDS is deducted in the year?
body.explanation: Annual rent is ₹75,000 × 12 = ₹9,00,000. At 10%, TDS is ₹90,000. She will receive a Form 131 certificate from the tenant every quarter.

children.text: Now look at her actual tax. Rent from property is taxed under "income from house property", where you deduct municipal taxes paid and then a flat 30% standard deduction for repairs and upkeep.

Her total income is within ₹12,00,000, so her tax is nil, yet ₹90,000 of her rent was withheld over the year. She can claim it all back as a refund, but a better option is to stop it at the source. As a senior citizen with nil tax, she can give the tenant Form 121 at the start of the year, or apply for a nil deduction certificate. Chapter 4 covers both.
Landlords and Tenants: Rent Paid by Individuals

markDefs.definition: Under the rule for individual tenants, TDS is deducted from the rent for the last month of the tax year, or the last month of the tenancy if it ends earlier, on the total rent for that period.

children.text: Salaried tenants paying more than
a month must deduct 2%, but not every month. The deduction is made
once

, from the rent for March or the final month of the tenancy, whichever comes first. The tenant deposits it using Form 141 with their PAN within 30 days from the end of that month, and gives the landlord a certificate in Form 132 (formerly Form 16C).

body.title: Quick Check: The March Rent
body.question: Tanvi stays all year and deducts ₹13,200 of TDS from her March rent. How much does she actually transfer to her landlord for March?
body.explanation: The whole year's TDS of ₹13,200 comes out of the single March payment, so she pays ₹55,000 minus ₹13,200 = ₹41,800. Landlords are often surprised by the small March transfer, so it is worth telling them in advance and sharing the Form 132 certificate.

body.title: What if the landlord has no PAN?

children.text: Without a valid PAN, the higher TDS rate of 20% applies under Section 397(2). For individual tenants, the rule carried over from the old Section 194-IB has one mercy: the TDS cannot exceed the rent for the last month of the year or tenancy. Even so, a landlord with no PAN usually cannot claim the credit, so ask for the PAN before signing the agreement.
The landlord's PAN also matters for your own tax: if you claim HRA exemption and pay more than ₹1,00,000 of rent in a year, you must report the landlord's PAN to your employer anyway.
Commission and Brokerage

Commission earners, such as property brokers, sub-brokers and distributors, face 2% TDS once a payer's commission to them crosses ₹20,000 in the year. Ramesh, a property broker in Thane, earns ₹60,000 from a builder for selling a flat. The builder deducts ₹1,200 and pays him ₹58,800. At only 2%, commission TDS rarely covers the actual tax, so commission earners usually owe more at filing time and should plan advance tax.

for professionals, declaring 50% of receipts as profit: ₹5,77,500. That is within the ₹12,00,000 rebate limit, so his tax is nil. The ₹48,000 his developer client deducted will come back only as a refund, after he files his return.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: TDS and GST
body.textWithBlank: Nikhil sends an invoice for ₹1,00,000 in fees plus ₹18,000 GST, shown separately. A client deducting 10% TDS should deduct ₹___.
body.explanation: When GST is shown separately on the invoice, TDS is calculated on the fee excluding GST, so 10% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹10,000, not 10% of ₹1,18,000. If a client deducts on the GST-inclusive amount, point this out before the next invoice.

body.title: Salaried employee vs freelancer: how TDS feels

columns.label: Salaried employee
points: One deductor who estimates your full-year tax
TDS roughly matches your final tax
Refunds and shortfalls are usually small

columns.label: Freelancer or landlord
points: Many deductors, none of whom see your full income
Flat rates that can be far above or below your tax
Quarterly Form 131 certificates from every payer, or Form 132 from individual tenants
Large refunds or large advance tax bills are common

body.title: Scenario: The Client Who Deducted but Did Not Report
body.scenario: In June 2027, Nikhil checks his Form 26AS before filing. His developer client's ₹48,000 of TDS is missing, even though every payment he received was 10% short. The client's accounts team says the tax "was deducted".
body.prompt: What could have gone wrong, and what should Nikhil do?
body.modelAnswer: Three things commonly go wrong: the client deducted but has not yet deposited the tax, deposited it but has not filed its quarterly Form 140 statements, or filed them against a wrong PAN. In all three cases the credit will not appear. Nikhil should ask the client for the Form 131 certificates for each quarter, which can only be generated after a correct statement is filed, along with the challan details. If the statement was wrong or not filed, the client must file or correct it. He should keep his invoices and bank statements showing the 10% short receipts, since under Section 401 he cannot be asked to pay tax that was actually deducted from him. If the credit still does not appear by the filing deadline, he can file on time and revise once it does. Chapter 5 covers this process in detail.

stats.label: Rent threshold
stats.context: 10% (property) or 2% (machinery) from businesses, 2% from individual tenants

children.text: Your Action Plan

body.title: For Landlords, Brokers and Freelancers
steps: List every tenant or client and note whether they are a business, an individual under audit, or an individual not under audit
For each, write down the applicable TDS row, rate and threshold from this lesson
Share your PAN on every rent agreement and invoice, and show GST separately
Collect Form 131 certificates every quarter from business payers, and Form 132 from individual tenants
Match every certificate against Form 26AS and AIS before filing
Estimate your actual tax. If TDS is far above it, plan Form 121 or a lower deduction certificate. If far below, plan advance tax

cards.definition: TDS on rent paid by businesses: 10% for land, building or furniture, 2% for plant and machinery, above ₹50,000 a month. Formerly 194-I.
TDS at 2% on rent above ₹50,000 a month paid by individuals and HUFs not under audit, deducted once. Formerly 194-IB.
TDS at 2% on commission or brokerage above ₹20,000 a year. Formerly 194H.
TDS on professional fees (10%) and technical services (2%) above ₹50,000 a year. Formerly 194J.
Quarterly TDS certificate from business deductors for non-salary payments. Formerly Form 16A.
TDS certificate issued after deducting through Form 141, such as by an individual tenant to a landlord. Formerly Form 16C.
Declaring 50% of gross receipts as profit without detailed books, for eligible resident professionals. Formerly Section 44ADA.

points: Businesses deduct 10% on property rent and 2% on machinery rent above ₹50,000 a month, while individual tenants deduct 2% once a year from the March or final rent
Commission above ₹20,000 a year attracts 2% TDS, and professional fees above ₹50,000 attract 10% (2% for technical services)
TDS is calculated on the fee excluding GST when GST is shown separately on the invoice
Flat TDS rates often bear no relation to your real tax: landlords and freelancers with low income get large refunds, while high earners on 2% rows owe more
Collect Form 131 or Form 132 certificates from every payer and match them to Form 26AS and AIS before filing
If TDS routinely exceeds your tax, use Form 121 or a lower deduction certificate instead of waiting for refunds
